Exposed once more in the Srebrenica camps, I take ship down the rivers and across the sea to Alexandria, where no one speaks my tongues; I trade in gesture, scale, and coin until the words come easier, and take the name Xene Drakos among the harbor's Greeks.

In an Alexandria debtor's market I recognize a tanner's ring on a starving boy's hand — Radoje's own grandson Dragan, sold off for his grandfather's debts — and some old, unaccountable guilt makes me weigh out coral enough to buy his freedom.
Marin Foscari teaches me to falsify the weights recorded in the Foscari Ledger when the harvest is thin, so that no household on our street goes hungry for want of an honest scale.

As my father once shaped me over the ledger, I shape the foundling Vuk from infancy in the Srebrenica camps, feeding him just enough truth and just enough lies that he wants nothing in the world but to serve me.

For all my new name and new tongue, I still weigh coral on my father's old bronze balance-scale rather than the steelyards the young factors favor — a small vanity that marks me instantly as a relic to anyone paying attention.

I read our marriage contract aloud to Beatriz Gundulić myself, in Latin, Slavic, and Italian in turn, so that she will understand exactly what she is promising away before her father's notary arrives.

Exposed as a monster in Ragusa, I flee inland with Beatriz Gundulić at my heels; among the strangers of Trebinje I talk my way past the gate-wardens with lies smoother than any contract and take the name Jelena Vranić.

Beatriz discovers what I have become and does not scream — instead she starts buying pig's blood from the butcher twice a week in her own name, and I drink it cold behind a shuttered cellar door while she keeps watch.

Fra Anzelmo climbs the stair to my rented room above the Customs House to hear confession from sailors too ashamed to kneel in the cathedral, and I listen through the wall to every sin they bring him.

Radoje the Tanner learns that Fra Anzelmo followed us out of Ragusa to drag me home for judgment, and turns our few Trebinje friends into a mob at our door — I stand as still as ash in the dark until the priest is alone, then break his neck to keep his mouth shut forever, and Beatriz and I flee by night toward the silver mines of Srebrenica.

Something wearing Fra Anzelmo's ruined shape claws up outside Alexandria's walls, sustained on whatever hatred survives a broken neck, and demands the confession he never got to hear; I recite it back to him in Latin, and he crumbles to nothing at last, satisfied.

The Voivode of Ash meets me on the Customs House stair on a night thick with fog, opens my throat with one grey finger, and drinks until I am no longer Ragusa's daughter but his — I wake with A Throat That Does Not Close and the taste of ash in my mouth forever after.
My skin dries to the grey of cold ash and I learn to stand as still as the Voivode himself, motionless in doorways until even rats forget I am there — I feel him settling further into my bones.
In Srebrenica's close camp, Beatriz's bought blood draws whispers within a week; I take up bandages instead and tend the mine's infirmary, learning to take my due from the wounded before they wake.

At a merchant's soiree I am led before a new silvered Murano mirror and see nothing where my face should be; a serving girl shrieks and the room turns on me before I fight free, and afterward I return in secret, playing physician to the wound I gave her, binding it myself to buy her silence.

After the mirror very nearly finishes me, I burn the last of the Foscari Ledger for kindling and wall off a cellar chamber beneath my warehouse with only a fist-sized breathing hole; Dragan sends me a mute boy named Ilya to keep watch over the bricks by day.

experiences.text: I am Ismenia, daughter of Marin Foscari, born in the free city of Ragusa in the year of Our Lord 1358; I keep my father's ledgers and haggle for coral and salt along the Adriatic wharves.

Exposed once more in the Srebrenica camps, I take ship down the rivers and across the sea to Alexandria, where no one speaks my tongues; I trade in gesture, scale, and coin until the words come easier, and take the name Xene Drakos among the harbor's Greeks.

In an Alexandria debtor's market I recognize a tanner's ring on a starving boy's hand — Radoje's own grandson Dragan, sold off for his grandfather's debts — and some old, unaccountable guilt makes me weigh out coral enough to buy his freedom.
Marin Foscari teaches me to falsify the weights recorded in the Foscari Ledger when the harvest is thin, so that no household on our street goes hungry for want of an honest scale.

As my father once shaped me over the ledger, I shape the foundling Vuk from infancy in the Srebrenica camps, feeding him just enough truth and just enough lies that he wants nothing in the world but to serve me.

For all my new name and new tongue, I still weigh coral on my father's old bronze balance-scale rather than the steelyards the young factors favor — a small vanity that marks me instantly as a relic to anyone paying attention.

I read our marriage contract aloud to Beatriz Gundulić myself, in Latin, Slavic, and Italian in turn, so that she will understand exactly what she is promising away before her father's notary arrives.

Beatriz discovers what I have become and does not scream — instead she starts buying pig's blood from the butcher twice a week in her own name, and I drink it cold behind a shuttered cellar door while she keeps watch.

I break ground on a vast chiming clockwork in my Bruges warehouse, telling the guild it will track the tides for my ships; secretly each gear is cut to mark out centuries, not hours, and no mortal mind but mine can guess why.

Fra Anzelmo climbs the stair to my rented room above the Customs House to hear confession from sailors too ashamed to kneel in the cathedral, and I listen through the wall to every sin they bring him.

Radoje the Tanner learns that Fra Anzelmo followed us out of Ragusa to drag me home for judgment, and turns our few Trebinje friends into a mob at our door — I stand as still as ash in the dark until the priest is alone, then break his neck to keep his mouth shut forever, and Beatriz and I flee by night toward the silver mines of Srebrenica.

Something wearing Fra Anzelmo's ruined shape claws up outside Alexandria's walls, sustained on whatever hatred survives a broken neck, and demands the confession he never got to hear; I recite it back to him in Latin, and he crumbles to nothing at last, satisfied.

The Voivode of Ash meets me on the Customs House stair on a night thick with fog, opens my throat with one grey finger, and drinks until I am no longer Ragusa's daughter but his — I wake with A Throat That Does Not Close and the taste of ash in my mouth forever after.
My skin dries to the grey of cold ash and I learn to stand as still as the Voivode himself, motionless in doorways until even rats forget I am there — I feel him settling further into my bones.
In Srebrenica's close camp, Beatriz's bought blood draws whispers within a week; I take up bandages instead and tend the mine's infirmary, learning to take my due from the wounded before they wake.

After the mirror very nearly finishes me, I burn the last of the Foscari Ledger for kindling and wall off a cellar chamber beneath my warehouse with only a fist-sized breathing hole; Dragan sends me a mute boy named Ilya to keep watch over the bricks by day.
